ety.text: Inherited from Middle English ugly, uggely, uglike, borrowed from Old Norse uggligr (“fearful, dreadful, horrible in appearance”), from uggr (“fear, apprehension, dread”) (possibly related to agg (“strife, hate”)), equivalent to ug + -ly. Cognate with Scots ugly, uglie, Icelandic ugglegur. Meaning softened to "very unpleasant to look at" around the late 14th century, and sense of "morally offensive" attested from around 1300.

senses.d: Displeasing to the eye; aesthetically unpleasing.
ex: the ugly view of his deformed crimes
O, I have passed a miserable night, / So full of ugly sights, of ghastly dreams.

senses.d: Displeasing to the ear or some other sense.
Offensive to one's sensibilities or morality.
ex: He played an ugly trick on us.
an ugly temper; to feel ugly

senses.d: Unpleasant; disagreeable; likely to cause trouble or loss.
ex: an ugly customer, wound or rumor
an ugly story that was being noised about in newsrooms across the nation
I want your ugly / I want your disease.

senses.d: Any product whose size and shape prevents it from fitting neatly on a pallet.
ex: Non-standard products (abnormal or 'uglies'): many distribution operations are designed to cater for standard palletized products.

senses.d: A shade for the face, projecting from a bonnet.
ex: […] camp-stools, telescopes, poetry-books, blue uglies, red petticoats, and parasols of every hue.

ety.text: From Middle French laid (“hideous, ugly”), from Old French laid, leid (“unpleasant, horrible, odious”), from Vulgar Latin *laitus (“unpleasant, ugly”), from Frankish *laiþ (“unpleasant, obstinate, odious”), from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz (“sorrowful, unpleasant”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“unpleasant”).
From moque, present indicative of moquer (“to mock”).
Inherited from Old French vilain, vilein, villein, from Late Latin vīllānus (“farm worker”), from Latin vīlla. Not related to vil.
Derived from Latin brūtus. Doublet of bruto.

Borrowed from Old French lait, leit (“unpleasant, horrible, odious”), of Germanic origin, from Low Frankish *laiþ (“unpleasant, obstinate, odious”) from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz (“sorrowful, unpleasant”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“unpleasant”).
From Latin foedus (“hideous”). According to Corominas borrowed from Asturian feu, displacing native hedo. Cognate with Portuguese feio. Compare English fedity.
From Old Galician-Portuguese feo (“ugly”), from Latin foedus (“hideous”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to frighten; be afraid”). Cognate with Galician feo, Asturian feu and Spanish feo.
From s- + gradevole. Compare Catalan and Spanish desagradable, French désagréable and Portuguese desagradável.
Literally, “Malay callus”. Used for the rhyme.
